result: The authors developed HABITS, a home-cage automated training system that enables free-moving mice to learn cognitive behaviors without human involvement. The system includes hardware components (cage, weighting platform, stimulus modules, lickports, pumps), a microcontroller-based programming framework, wireless connectivity, and GUI for remote monitoring. Over 100 units were built at less than $100 each, and mice were trained for up to 3 months in various paradigms.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the system design and implementation. Reviewer 1 called it 'a new and important system' with 'a robust system' and 'task flexibility.' Reviewer 2 described it as 'simple yet elegant design' and noted 'the data are strong, the arguments are convincing.' Reviewer 3 celebrated 'an inexpensively constructed, replicable training environment.' The editor stated the authors 'provide convincing evidence in support of the tasks they developed.'

result: Autonomous training in HABITS was compared to manual training in the d2AFC task. All 10 mice in autonomous training learned the task within 15 days, achieving 980±25 trials/day. Autonomous training required more trials (10,164±1062 vs. 6845±782) but fewer days than manual training. Autonomous training resulted in higher water consumption (1.65±0.06 vs. 0.97±0.03 ml/day) and maintained body weight comparable to free water controls, while manual training showed sharp body weight drops.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically highlighted 'comparison of manual-like training vs constant training' as a strength. Reviewer 3 found this comparison 'intriguing' and noted that 'manual training resulted in significantly faster learning, in almost half the number of trials on average.' The reviewers accepted the data showing trade-offs between training methods, with no challenges to the validity of these comparative findings.

result: HABITS successfully trained mice on multiple sensory modalities including sound orientation (10 mice), light orientation (11 mice), and light color (8 mice) discrimination tasks. Light color discrimination was most challenging (82,932±6817 trials), consistent with limited mouse wavelength sensitivity. RT-2AFC, random foraging, and dynamic foraging tasks were also successfully implemented, with the dynamic foraging task being the first demonstration in fully autonomous training for freely moving mice.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'comparison of varying cue types' as a strength. Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the complexity of behavioral phenotypes one can collect using this relatively inexpensive ($100/box) and high-throughput procedure.' The editor stated the system captures 'a variety of complex behaviors.' No reviewer challenged the validity of these multi-modal training demonstrations.

result: Mice exhibited clear nocturnal behavior with trial peaks at the beginning and end of dark periods. More than two-thirds of trials occurred in blocks >5 trials, with >55% having inter-trial intervals <2s. Performance increased with block length, suggesting greater task engagement during longer blocks. Light color modality showed slightly lower dark-period trial percentage (57.89±3.18% vs. >66%), possibly due to light stimulus effects on circadian rhythms.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically mentioned 'circadian analysis' as a strength. Reviewer 2 initially raised concerns about 'inter-trial intervals can vary significantly' and task engagement, but noted in their revision comments that 'The authors now provide information regarding task engagement of the mice across a 24 hour cycle' and that their concerns were 'adequately addressed.' This circadian and engagement analysis was accepted by all reviewers.

result: All 8 mice underwent contingency reversal training for an average of 52.25±16.39 times, with one mouse achieving 125 reversals in 113 days. Most mice (6/8) showed learning-to-learn effects, gradually decreasing trials needed to reach criterion across reversals. The average trials to criterion was highly correlated with first reversal performance, representing individual cognitive ability.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 highlighted 'long-term measurement' as a strength. Reviewer 3 noted that 'mice may require durations of training far longer than laboratories are able to invest with manual training (up to over 100k trials, over months of daily testing) but that the tasks are achievable.' The extensive reversal learning data was accepted without challenge as demonstrating the system's capability for long-term cognitive assessment.

result: HABITS successfully trained mice on complex cognitive tasks including evidence accumulation (8/10 mice), multimodal integration (13/15 mice with sound/multimodal stimuli), and confidence-probing tasks (5/6 mice). Mice showed expected behavioral patterns: longer sample periods and higher contrast improved performance in evidence accumulation; mice favored earlier stimuli in multimodal integration; time investment differed between correct and incorrect trials in confidence-probing, modulated by stimulus contrast.
evaluation: The editor stated the system demonstrates 'the utility of a machine learning approach to expedite the acquisition of task demands' and captures 'a variety of complex behaviors.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the complexity of behavioral phenotypes one can collect' and that 'the data are strong, the arguments are convincing.' These complex cognitive paradigms were accepted as valid demonstrations of the system's capabilities.

result: In continuous learning experiments, mice quickly switched between tasks with learning rates following modality difficulty. Reversal of sound frequency (pro to anti) required significantly longer learning than sound orientation reversal. Mice showed higher reaction times when encountering new tasks, gradually decreasing with training, suggesting a strategy of responding slowly to learn quickly. Mice exhibited large bias at the beginning of each task, initially acquiring reward from one lickport before gradually switching to follow current stimuli.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'task flexibility' as a strength. Reviewer 2 stated 'the data are strong, the arguments are convincing.' Reviewer 3 noted that the system allows investigators to examine how 'the process of learning a task has been repeatedly shown to be different' across conditions. The continuous learning findings were accepted without methodological challenges.

result: HABITS successfully trained mice on novel paradigms including dDMS (10/10 mice, 64.45±7.88 days, >120,000 trials), d3AFC (14/14 mice in 13.85±1.05 days for frequency-based; 45.16±11.46 days for orientation-based), and context-dependent attention tasks (6/6 mice, 48.09±7.54 days). Performance showed expected patterns: delay-dependent decrements in dDMS, proximity-based errors in d3AFC, and conflict-dependent performance reductions in attention tasks.
evaluation: The editor emphasized the system's ability to capture 'a variety of complex behaviors.' Reviewer 1 stated 'I find no major problems with this report.' Reviewer 2 noted 'the complexity of behavioral phenotypes one can collect' and that 'the data are strong.' Reviewer 3 celebrated the system's ability to train mice on tasks that 'may require durations of training far longer than laboratories are able to invest with manual training.' These novel paradigms were accepted as valid demonstrations.

result: HABITS incorporates a machine-teaching (MT) algorithm that optimizes trial presentation, leading to more efficient training and higher-quality behavioral outcomes. In working memory tasks, MT-trained mice achieved criteria with significantly fewer trials than random controls (3/8 random mice failed to reach criteria in 60 days). MT training exhibited curriculum learning trajectories, reduced bias, minimized reliance on noise variables, and increased reliance on current stimuli. This is claimed as the first demonstration of machine teaching in real-world animal training.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically highlighted 'machine teaching' as a strength. Reviewer 2 stated 'the authors include a machine learning algorithm to correct for erroneous strategies that mice develop which is incredibly elegant and important for this approach' and that 'the data are strong, the arguments are convincing.' The editor noted the system 'demonstrate the utility of a machine learning approach to expedite the acquisition of task demands.' All reviewers accepted the MT algorithm as a significant contribution.

result: In multi-dimensional tasks, both MT and random groups achieved >80% correct rates, but MT showed significantly higher learning rates and faster forgetting of irrelevant cues during the second goal (orientation to frequency transition). MT quickly suppressed sensitivity to irrelevant modalities while maintaining low noise sensitivity, resulting in a circuitous learning path. MT-trained mice exhibited significantly lower left/right and stay/switch biases in testing, suggesting more stable and task-aligned behavioral training.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 emphasized that the MT algorithm is 'incredibly elegant and important for this approach, as mice will develop odd strategies when given complete freedom' and that it effectively 'correct[s] for erroneous strategies.' Reviewer 1 noted 'machine teaching' as a strength with no concerns. The multi-dimensional task results demonstrating MT's superiority in complex scenarios were accepted without challenge.

result: The study presents an extensive behavioral dataset from ~300 mice trained and tested in more than 20 diverse paradigms, consisting of entire learning trajectories with well-documented training strategies and behavioral outcomes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically noted 'high n's' as a strength. Reviewer 2 stated 'I think the manuscript will be highly cited given the complexity of behavioral phenotypes one can collect' and emphasized the 'high-throughput procedure.' Reviewer 3 noted the system's utility 'for other investigators interested in studying mouse cognition.' The scale and comprehensiveness of the dataset was recognized and valued by all reviewers.

result: Suboptimal strategies like biases are common among expert mice trained in various paradigms, potentially stemming from exploration in real-world uncertain environments.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted that 'the strategic uses of side biases in mice, as in primates, can benefit learning, rather than side biases solely being a problem,' acknowledging the complexity of bias in animal learning. Reviewer 2 emphasized the importance of the MT algorithm to 'correct for erroneous strategies that mice develop.' The existence and relevance of suboptimal strategies was accepted by reviewers.
